Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow.

Learning a Second Language

1. Most Indians grow up hearing more than one language. A child in Bengaluru may speak Kannada with friends, Tamil at home and English at school, switching between them without a second thought. For much of the world, where people speak only one language, this would seem remarkable. In India, it is ordinary.

2. Researchers have long studied what this does to the brain. Many studies suggest that people who regularly use two or more languages are better at focusing attention and switching between tasks. Because they must constantly choose which language to use, their brains get regular practice in control and flexibility.

3. There are social benefits as well. A second language opens the door to another culture – its songs, jokes and ways of seeing the world. People who speak the language of their neighbours are more likely to understand and trust them. In a diverse country, this can be a quiet force for unity.

4. Yet many young people are losing their mother tongues. Urban parents, eager for their children to master English, sometimes stop speaking their own language at home. Within a generation, a family can lose a language that its ancestors spoke for centuries, and with it a store of stories, proverbs and knowledge.

5. Experts argue that the choice need not be either-or. Children can learn English well while keeping their mother tongue strong, especially if they are encouraged to read and write it, not only speak it. A language, they remind us, is not merely a tool for jobs. It is a home for memory.

(i) How many languages might a child in Bengaluru speak, according to the passage?  (a) One  (b) Three – Kannada, Tamil and English  (c) Five  (d) Two
(ii) Why does the writer call multilingualism "ordinary" in India?
(iii) What mental advantage do multilingual people have, according to studies?
(iv) Why do bilinguals' brains get "regular practice in control"?  (a) They read less  (b) They avoid speaking  (c) They must constantly choose which language to use  (d) They sleep more
(v) Which word in paragraph 2 means "the ability to change or adapt easily"?  (a) flexibility  (b) practice  (c) attention  (d) control
(vi) Name one social benefit of learning a second language.
(vii) In a diverse country, a shared language can be …  (a) useless  (b) a barrier  (c) a cause of war  (d) a quiet force for unity
(viii) Why are some urban children losing their mother tongues?
(ix) What is lost along with a language?  (a) Money  (b) Stories, proverbs and knowledge  (c) Schools  (d) Land
(x) Which earlier lesson in Flamingo shares the concern of paragraph 4?
(xi) How can children keep their mother tongue strong?
(xii) What does "It is a home for memory" mean?
items.answer: (i) (b) Three – Kannada, Tamil and English (ii) Most Indians grow up hearing and using more than one language. (iii) They are better at focusing attention and switching between tasks. (iv) (c) They must constantly choose which language to use (v) (a) flexibility (vi) Opens a door to another culture / helps understand and trust neighbours / promotes unity. (vii) (d) a quiet force for unity (viii) Parents stop speaking it at home in their eagerness for children to master English. (ix) (b) Stories, proverbs and knowledge (x) "The Last Lesson" – the value of one's mother tongue. (xi) By reading and writing it, not only speaking it. (xii) A language holds a community's history, culture and memories.

The Quiet Return of Board Games

1. In an age of smartphones and streaming, one might expect board games to have quietly disappeared. Instead, the opposite has happened. In cities across India, cafés devoted to board games have opened, and sales of strategy games have risen steadily for a decade. Young professionals who spend all day in front of screens are, it seems, hungry for something they can touch.

2. Part of the appeal is social. A board game requires people to sit at the same table, face one another and talk. Unlike an online game, in which players may never meet, a board game turns an evening into a shared event. Researchers who study play suggest that this face-to-face contact satisfies a need that digital communication cannot fully meet.

3. There is also the pleasure of thinking. Many modern board games demand planning, negotiation and the ability to predict what an opponent will do. Teachers have noticed that students who play such games regularly become more patient and better at solving problems. Some schools now keep a shelf of games in the library for wet afternoons.

4. Traditional Indian games have shared in this revival. Chaupar, pallanguzhi and ludo – itself a descendant of the ancient game of pachisi – are being redesigned with attractive boards and sold to a new generation. Grandparents who once played them on the floor of a courtyard are now teaching the rules to grandchildren in high-rise flats.

5. Not everyone is convinced the trend will last. Critics point out that many board-game cafés are expensive and attract mostly the well-off. Yet supporters argue that a simple board and a few counters cost very little. What matters, they say, is not the price of the game but the willingness to switch off the screen and sit down together.

The Return of Millets

1. For thousands of years, millets such as jowar, bajra and ragi fed much of India. They grew on dry land with little water and needed few chemicals. But after the Green Revolution of the 1960s, rice and wheat spread across the country, supported by irrigation and government purchase. Millets came to be seen as "poor people's food" and their cultivation fell sharply.

2. Today, millets are making a comeback. Nutrition experts point out that they are rich in fibre, iron and calcium, and release sugar slowly into the blood, which makes them valuable in a country with rising rates of diabetes. The United Nations declared 2023 the International Year of Millets, following a proposal by India.

3. Millets are also climate-friendly. As rainfall becomes less predictable, crops that survive drought matter more. Millets need far less water than rice and can grow in poor soil. For farmers in dry regions, they offer security when other crops fail.

4. Challenges remain. Many urban consumers do not know how to cook millets, and processing them is harder than polishing rice. Prices for farmers are often low because there are few buyers. Some state governments now include millets in school meals and public distribution, creating a steady demand.

5. Chefs and food start-ups have helped too, turning ragi and jowar into biscuits, pasta and breakfast cereals. Whether millets will regain their old place on Indian plates remains to be seen. But for the first time in decades, the humble grain is being talked about with respect.
